question.problem:
Let $F(x)=2{x}^{3}$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{2}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{2} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩} \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
